body_markdown:
My darling wife Maire Anne and I took three mini-vacations in September. The first was four days in Truro (the northern end of Cape Cod) over our 42nd anniversary. The second was an overnight on tiny Cuttyhunk Island at the end of the small Elizabeth Islands chain off the southern coast of the Cape, where singer-songwriter me had a gig at an artist’s retreat. The third was a night in Gloucester (north shore) to see a dear friend. For all of these, we took Maire Anne’s 2013 Honda Fit, which, as I’ve said before, is the car we take when we want to arrive somewhere with “no stories.” I mean, I love my daily-driver 2003 BMW E39 530i, but the idea that the 23-year-old 220,000-mile BMW is more reliable than a 13-year-old 85,000-mile Honda is somewhere between denial and delusion.


So… funny story.


While driving home from Gloucester, the Honda began making some light grinding noises from the right front that got louder when turning. Since the braking itself seemed fine and the car wasn’t pulling to one side, I assumed the noise was something like a rust flake rubbing on the rotor, or a CV joint or a wheel bearing going bad. But as we neared home, braking itself began generating the grinding sound, so I knocked off the final ten miles slowly and carefully.


When I got home, I put the Fit in the hallowed spot over the mid-rise lift (it has some other deferred maintenance issues I need to deal with), pulled off the wheels, and immediately saw that the right-side brake rotor was scored, which I would’ve seen through the wheels had I stopped and looked through the slots. Looking at it further, I was astonished to find that one of the right-side pads was worn down to the metal, the other was paper-thin, and unlike every other car I’ve owned that was built in the last 30 years, the Fit doesn’t have pad-wear sensors. This was all remarkably careless of me. If you’d asked me if I’d inspected the brake pads when I swapped wheels in the spring, I would’ve looked you straight in the eye and said: “Of course!” Live and learn.


Yeesh!


Rob Siegel


I hopped online and ordered pads and rotors, and began the required disassembly. I pulled off the calipers, began to unscrew the two Phillips screws holding each rotor to its hub, and immediately ran into a wall.


Nearly every car with disc brakes has one or two of these set-screws holding the rotor to the hub. On the BMWs I’m most familiar with, there’s a single Allen-head fastener instead of two Phillips, but whichever style your car has, they all share the same three annoying qualities:


1. It’s very common for the threads to be seized.
2. The Phillips grooves and Allen hex hole can easily strip if you use too much force.
3. The screw heads are recessed so the wheel can mount flush to the rotor/hub flange. This makes it difficult to get heat and/or penetrating oil onto the threads, and impossible to grab the fastener from the sides with Vise Grips if you strip the grooves or hex hole.


When undoing fasteners, I always look at the thing I’m about to remove, judge it by the metric “If this strips or breaks, will I be in a world of pain?” and if so, *PROCEED WITH EXTREME CAUTION* . The mantra is that you shouldn’t just crank down on a fastener and increase the torque until it turns. As the old song goes, when an immovable object meets an irresistible force, something’s gotta give. It might be rusty, seized threads that let go of their death grip, but it might also be a bolt that snaps or a fastener that rounds off its corners. Sometimes you don’t care, but in this case, you definitely do.


Phillips screws generally aren’t used for high-torque applications, as they’re very prone to having their grooves stripped. This can be caused by a worn-out or low-quality screwdriver tip or driver bit, cheap screws, not having the driver bit square with the screw head, not pushing in with enough pressure to keep it seated, or a combination. But when they’re difficult to get off, the root cause is almost always that the threads are seized. You don’t really have much hope without penetrating oil and heat, but the recessed nature of the rotor fasteners means that penetrating oil is unlikely to get into the threads, and[an induction heater](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/adventures-in-induction-heater-land/) is of no help because you can’t put it around any part of the fastener. That leaves only heat delivered by a torch, but even there, you’re heating the part that’s furthest from the threads and hoping that enough heat gets down where it’s needed. Plus, the last thing you want is for the thing to get so hot that the head of the fastener is red taffy, as when you twist a bit in the Phillips slots, they may deform.


For rotor screws like these, you never want to grab some random old pointy-tipped Phillips screwdriver or some used-up driver bit. You want to make sure it’s a high-quality #3 screwdriver or bit with a flat nose. If it’s an Allen-key fastener, I’ll clean the hole with a pick, tap in the Allen socket, and spin it out with the impact wrench. This usually works, but if it doesn’t, you feel like an idiot because you’ve instantly rounded the corners off the hole. With Phillips fasteners, I never *ever* use an impact wrench, as that’s just a recipe for the threads to strip instantly, in which case you have little choice but to drill out the head of the bolt. Fortunately, if this happens, it’s not as bad as with other fasteners, as you usually can just drill or grind off the part of the head that’s in the recess, and once you can pull the rotor off, there’s usually enough of the screw standing proud of the hub surface that you can oil and heat it and twist it out with Vise Grips.


So, in approaching the screws on the Honda’s rotors, I used a new DeWalt #3 bit on a little ¼” breaker bar. I pressed directly inward and applied torque. None of the four of them moved. I sprayed them with SiliKroil (not that it can easily reach the threads) and heated them with the MAPP gas torch. I did this three times, each time coming right up to the point where I thought the grooves might strip, and got nowhere.


Heat is almost always helpful with stuck fasteners, but it’s less effective with recessed screws.


Rob Siegel


So I did what anyone would do and went on YouTube. I found a tip to use a hammer on something like a 3/8” ratchet extension to tap the recessed screw head and try to shock the threads into letting go. I tried it several times, and it made no difference.


Then I saw videos make use of a tool that’s uniquely valuable for this application—the hand impact driver. This is a cylinder about the size of a toilet paper tube with a spring-loaded twist mechanism inside. You load the tip of it with the needed Phillips or Allen bit, position it on the fastener, and smack the other end with a hammer. Not only does it translate the inward smack into a loosening twist, but the hammer-smack also increases the bite of the bit onto the fastener you’re trying to loosen in a way that an air or electric impact wrench doesn’t, making it less likely to strip. Genius, right?


One of dozens of hand impact drivers available online.


Amazon/Aiourx


I hopped online with the intent of buying one of these with next-day delivery. I saw that most of them come with a variety of Phillips, slotted, and hex bits, but a few of them instead have square drivers to put sockets on. This struck me as strange. I mean, if you have a stuck nut or a bolt, you wouldn’t need the smack-it-with-a-hammer-and-it-also-pushes-the-tool-into-the-fastener thing—you’d just spin it off with an impact wrench.


But then a funny thing happened: My brain did that funny pattern-matching thing that it sometimes does, and I realized that I had one of these in my big tool chest in the corner of the garage (the tools I use constantly are in a smaller chest closer to the cars). I have no idea where it came from and I’d never used it, but I dug around and found it. It had a ½” drive on it, so to use a Phillips bit, I had to put 1/2” to 3/8” and 3/8” to ¼” adapters on it, then a little socket on it to hold the Phillips bit, all of which made it ungainly to hold and smack.


Rotate it 90 degrees and it looks like the Saturn V rocket.


Rob Siegel


Holding it and smacking it a few times with a hammer got the screws on the left rotor out, but the ones on the right rotor did not go so easily into the dumpster. Those required a sequential application of three heat-and-smack cycles before they surrendered.


Booya!


Rob Siegel


So, the hand impact driver is totally the right tool to remove these recessed Phillips brake rotor fasteners, and I’ll buy one that directly accepts the bits and doesn’t need the ungainly adapters. However, Professor Hack wants to make sure that you know that the larger issue is that if a fastener like this isn’t coming out, you should stop before you strip or round it, because if you don’t, you’re only going to create a lot more work for yourself. I’m as susceptible to “mechanic’s red mist” as the next person. I was glad I had the patience to deal with these little buggers correctly. The solution to not having to do this next time? Anti-seize.


And yes, I promise to check the brake pads on all my cars.


***
